title: Risk Treatment
summary: Risk treatment is the decision and the action taken in response to an identified risk, and formal frameworks reduce it to four options: avoid the activity, reduce the risk with controls, transfer it to another party such as an insurer, or accept it with a named owner and a review date. Choosing the option is a business decision recorded in the risk register, not a technical judgement made once and then forgotten. In practice treatment shows up as control projects, contract clauses, insurance policies and formal acceptances, each carrying a cost and leaving some residual risk behind. The mistake people make is to treat acceptance as doing nothing, because an accepted risk with no owner, no rationale and no expiry is simply an unmanaged risk that everyone has quietly agreed to ignore.

beginner.definition: Risk treatment is what you decide to do about a risk you have found. In most frameworks there are four main choices. You can avoid the activity, reduce the risk, pass it to someone else, or accept it. Accepting a risk is a real decision and needs a name against it.
beginner.whyItMatters: Finding a risk is not the same as dealing with it. Without a clear decision, problems stay open for years and nobody is responsible. Some risks are cheaper to move than to fix, such as buying insurance. Others must be reduced because the possible harm is too large. A written treatment choice makes the cost and the owner visible.
howItWorks: List each identified risk with its cause, its possible impact, and the owner of the area.
Compare the treatment options and their cost against the value of the activity.
Choose one option and record who decided, why, and when the choice will be reviewed.
Carry out the chosen controls, and set a date to confirm they work as expected.
Track the risk that remains after treatment, called residual risk, against your appetite.
Close the entry only when the risk is gone or a new decision replaces it.
beginner.example: Imagine you rent a flat and you are going away for a month. You can cancel the trip, which avoids the risk. You can fit a stronger lock, which reduces it. You can ask a neighbour to look in, which moves part of the risk. Or you can accept it and leave the flat empty. Whichever you choose, you write down who is checking and when you return.
takeaways: Treatment is a decision with an owner, a reason, and a review date.
Accepting a risk is valid only when someone accountable says so.
Always record the risk that remains after the controls are in place.

objectives: List the four common risk treatment options and explain what each one means.
Explain the difference between reducing a risk and transferring it.
Describe what makes an accepted risk a managed decision rather than neglect.
Explain how residual risk is compared with the organisation's risk appetite.
Outline how treatment decisions are recorded, reviewed and closed.
